# What would happen to the newspapers?

## Where the man appears and what he is doing

The man in the grey v-neck t-shirt is in the closing shot of the video, roughly
from 0:97 to 0:108 (his hand and forearm enter frame around 97–99 s, his full body
from about 100 s, and his face — he wears dark-framed glasses — is clearly visible
from about 103 s until the picture fades to black just after 108 s). This is the
end of the Vanuatu Daily Post "Running the Press" piece.

He is standing in an open-sided shed with the roller door open onto a yard, at the
far end of a long, narrow wooden trestle bench. Laid out along the whole length of
that bench is a long shingled run of freshly printed newspaper sheets — overlapping
each other like roof tiles, with the printer's colour registration bars (yellow,
red, blue blocks) visible down the exposed strips. The sheets are wider than the
narrow bench top, so their long edges droop slightly over both sides of it. At his
end the run bunches up into a thicker pile whose end sits on, and just short of,
the end of the bench.

He is leaning over the bench and working the pile with both hands: his far hand is
laid flat on top of the run, lifting and peeling back the corner of a top sheet,
and his near hand is pinching and squaring the near corner of the stack at the end
of the bench. It is an aligning, smoothing and checking action — tidying the pile
and looking at the sheets — not a lifting or carrying action.

## The answer

**If he stepped back three feet and took his hands off, essentially nothing would
happen to the newspapers. They would simply stay exactly where they are, lying on
the bench.**

The reason is that the bench, not the man, is bearing the weight. The papers rest
flat on a horizontal, stable surface that supports them along their entire length,
and the pile sits on the bench top rather than overhanging its end. His hands are
resting on top of the stack and pressing sideways/downward on it; they are not
holding it up, holding it back, or keeping it from tipping. Take those hands away
and gravity is given nothing new to act on — the stack is already at rest and
already fully supported, so it stays at rest.

The only visible changes would be small and confined to the spot he happened to be
touching:

- The top sheet whose corner he has peeled up into an arch would flop back down
  flat onto the pile.
- The end of the stack he was squaring up would be left slightly fanned, splayed
  or untidy instead of straightened — the shingled edges would stay uneven rather
  than snapping into alignment.
- If he was mid-push, the papers would stop moving immediately rather than sliding
  on; newsprint is light and the friction between the sheets and against the bench
  is more than enough to kill any momentum instantly.

What would *not* happen: the newspapers would not fall to the floor, slide off the
end of the bench, topple over, collapse, scatter, or blow away as a consequence of
him stepping back. There is no stored tension or stacked instability that his hands
are restraining.

## Two qualifications

First, the sheets are very light loose newsprint and the roller door beside him is
wide open. A gust of wind through that doorway could lift or riffle the top sheets
— but that would be the wind doing it, not his stepping back, and it could happen
just as easily while he is standing there.

Second, this holds because the run of paper is supported by the bench along its
length. If some of the pile had been overhanging the end of the bench and was being
propped by his hands or body, that overhanging portion would droop and slide off
when he moved away. From what is visible in the shot, the pile stops at or just
before the end of the bench, so this does not apply here.
